analysis.one_liner: Limits judges' power to seal court records and approve secret settlements that hide public health and safety dangers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on April 8, 2003, drew no cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies get sued over dangerous products, the cases often end with two kinds of secrecy: judges seal the evidence, and settlement agreements include gag clauses forbidding anyone from ever discussing what happened. This bill would have put strict limits on both. A judge could only keep health-or-safety information hidden after making specific public findings that secrecy serves a substantial interest, and settlements could no longer stop anyone from reporting hazards to government regulators or from discussing the case. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers who could be harmed by dangerous products. The bill would have made it far harder to bury evidence of defects, drug hazards, or safety problems inside sealed court files and confidential settlements — information that today often never reaches regulators, journalists, or future victims. Injury victims and the public would also keep the right to tell federal and state agencies what they learned in litigation, no matter what a settlement said.

how_it_helps.text: Courts could no longer seal records or approve secret settlements that hide information relevant to public health or safety unless the judge first finds, on the record, that the public interest in disclosure is outweighed by a specific and substantial confidentiality interest.

Parties could no longer be gagged from reporting safety information to federal or state agencies that enforce the laws covering it — for example, a plaintiff who learned of a drug hazard in a lawsuit could still tell the FDA.

Settlement agreements could not forbid a party from saying a settlement happened, from stating its terms (other than the dollar amount), or from discussing case evidence involving public health or safety, unless a judge makes specific findings for secrecy.
The party asking for secrecy would bear the burden of proving it deserves an exception, shifting the default from silence to disclosure.

analysis.who_pays: Companies facing product-liability and personal-injury suits — especially drug makers, medical device makers, automakers, and manufacturers of consumer products — along with their insurers. Secret settlements are a tool for resolving claims quickly and cheaply while keeping damaging safety information out of competitors' hands, regulators' files, and the news; this bill would have removed that tool in any case touching health or safety.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes it harder to keep anything secret in a civil case that touches health or safety, which could expose legitimately confidential business information, trade secrets, and private medical or personal records that appear in discovery even when they pose no public hazard.

Companies settle cases on the understanding that the matter ends quietly; requiring public disclosure of settlement terms could make defendants fight longer and settle for less, which could leave some injured people with slower or smaller recoveries.

Federal judges already have discretion under existing court rules to refuse overbroad secrecy orders, so supporters of the status quo argue a new federal statute is a blunt instrument for a problem better handled by judges weighing each case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: lawsuits are how the public learns about unsafe products, and gag clauses have kept information about health hazards locked inside courthouse files. The costs are also real — the bill would make some settlements harder to reach, could expose business information that is genuinely confidential rather than dangerous, and federalizes a decision that judges currently make case by case. The bill tries to limit this by allowing secrecy when a court finds a specific, substantial privacy interest that outweighs public safety and by keeping agency disclosures confidential. On balance, the transparency gain for the public outweighs the added friction for defendants, but the bill was never debated, so those trade-offs were never tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the bill on April 8, 2003, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill carried only one sponsor for its entire two-year life.
The action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate defendants in product-liability and personal-injury cases are better off: secret settlements and sealed court records remain available to keep safety information out of public view.

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 2003 and delivered introductory remarks on it; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 21 months of the Congress.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled whether the bill received a hearing or markup; none was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a partisan fight; a Democrat introduced it, no one else — from either party — cosponsored it, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee simply never acted.

industries.note: These companies face the largest share of product-liability suits involving health hazards, and secrecy orders have historically let settlement documents describing drug and device dangers stay under seal. The bill would force that information into the open, so the industry's interest in quiet settlements runs against the public's interest in knowing about hazards.

Defective-product litigation often turns on internal documents about known safety problems; the bill would let those documents and settlement terms become public rather than sealed, raising the cost of concealing known defects from regulators and future buyers.

industries.industry: Liability insurers and corporate defense bar
industries.note: Confidentiality clauses are a standard tool for resolving liability claims quickly and cheaply; restricting them makes cases harder to settle quietly and increases defense costs, which can be passed to policyholders and consumers.
